Environmental factors appear to play a significant role in primary systemic vasculitis, as suggested by several studies retrieved from local healthcare Q&A matches. While the exact mechanisms are not fully understood, it is clear that exposure to certain environmental substances and conditions can increase the risk of developing this condition.

These studies indicate associations between farming, silica, solvents, allergy, and various forms of systemic vasculitis (PSV). Additionally, research suggests that antiphospholipid antibodies may also be linked to environmental factors in some cases.

However, it is essential to note that incorporating an adjustment for corticosteroid use in some studies failed to show a link between the presence of antiphospholipid antibodies and the development of primary systemic vasculitis. Nonetheless, these findings highlight the potential importance of considering environmental factors in the diagnosis and management of this condition.

Furthermore, active travel has been shown to be associated with physical environmental characteristics, suggesting that individuals who engage in active travel may benefit from increased levels of physical activity to improve their overall health outcomes.
